sections.text:
The first half of Daniel (chapters 1 to 6) tells of Daniel and his friends as exiles serving at foreign courts: the blazing furnace, the writing on the wall, the lions’ den. In each story they stay faithful under pressure and God proves to be above every king.

The second half (7 to 12) records visions of empires rising and falling, of one like a son of man receiving an everlasting kingdom, and of the dead being raised.

The book is set in the sixth century before Christ, and the traditional view is that Daniel wrote it then. Many scholars think it reached its final form in the second century, during the persecution under Antiochus IV. Part of it is written in Aramaic. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include additional passages.

Jesus’ title for himself, the Son of Man, draws on chapter 7. Christians agree that the visions declare God’s rule over history. They differ widely on the details: which empires are meant, how to count the seventy weeks of chapter 9, and how much refers to the time of Antiochus, to the first coming of Christ or to the end.
